scenes.tts: This cell has copied every chromosome. Each daughter must get exactly one copy of each. But one chromosome is attached to only one pole. And the whole cell waits for it. What is it waiting for?
scenes.visual: THE ONE WORLD appears at once: a cell in cross-section filling the frame (grey oval), a yellow pole at far left and far right, grey spindle fibres between them that keep growing and shrinking. Two duplicated chromosomes (blue sister rods, teal cohesin rings, orange kinetochore dots) sit at the middle, each gripped from both poles and jiggling gently. A third, THE STUCK ONE, sits near the left pole: its left kinetochore is attached to the left pole, its right kinetochore is free and pulses red. A red dashed wave travels from that free kinetochore to the PANEL at top right: a purple clamp labelled 'anaphase brake' beside a red lamp reading 'WAIT'. Counter under the lamp: 'empty kinetochores: 1' (it counts what is drawn). On 'What is it waiting for?' the question appears as large text over the upper frame and stays to the end of the scene.
scenes.narration: This cell has copied every chromosome. Each daughter must get exactly one copy of each. But one chromosome is attached to only one pole. And the whole cell waits for it. What is it waiting for?

scenes.visual: Title 'What the Cell Waits For' over the same world, which keeps moving: fibres flicker, the red wave keeps pulsing to the panel.

scenes.tts: Look closer at one copied chromosome. Two sister chromatids lie side by side, held by cohesin rings. Each sister carries a kinetochore, the patch where spindle fibres grip. The two face opposite ways.
scenes.visual: Camera eases in on THE HERO, the upper of the two middle chromosomes, until it fills about 60% of frame height (in the zoom it has no fibres yet: they retract as the camera arrives). Show then tell: the two blue rods settle first, then teal rings are seen along the arms and at the centromere, then the two orange kinetochores glow on opposite faces. Labels as named: 'sister chromatids' (blue), 'cohesin' (teal), 'kinetochore' (orange, twice). Gentle breathing motion on the rods.
scenes.narration: Look closer at one copied chromosome. Two sister chromatids lie side by side, held by cohesin rings. Each sister carries a kinetochore, the patch where spindle fibres grip. The two face opposite ways.

scenes.tts: Fibres reach the kinetochores at random. The goal is biorientation, each sister gripped by the opposite pole. But both sisters can be gripped by the same pole. That is syntelic, an error.
scenes.visual: Camera pulls back just enough to show both yellow poles at the frame edges. Grey fibre tips probe toward the hero from both poles, missing and retracting. A ghost preview (50% opacity) briefly shows the goal: left kinetochore to left pole, right kinetochore to right pole, label 'biorientation' (blue). The ghost fades. Then what actually happens: two fibres from the LEFT pole catch both kinetochores (the right kinetochore twists round to face left). Label 'syntelic' (red). The hero slides a little toward the left pole.
scenes.narration: Fibres reach the kinetochores at random. The goal is biorientation, each sister gripped by the opposite pole. But both sisters can be gripped by the same pole. That is syntelic, an error.

scenes.tts: How can a cell tell right from wrong? It can sense force. Think of the pair as a short rope, with cohesin resisting. Pulled from opposite ends, it goes taut. That stretch is tension.
scenes.visual: Camera pans down to the OTHER middle chromosome, already bioriented. Its two sisters are pulled toward opposite poles (yellow arrows on each fibre); the teal rings strain; the gap between its two kinetochores visibly lengthens. A blue bracket spans the two kinetochores and grows with the stretch, label 'tension (schematic)'. For the rope line, a faint rope outline is laid over the pair for 3 s, taut between two pull arrows, then fades back into the chromosome.
scenes.narration: How can a cell tell right from wrong? It can sense force. Think of the pair as a short rope, with cohesin resisting. Pulled from opposite ends, it goes taut. That stretch is tension.

scenes.tts: Now go back to the syntelic pair. Both sisters are pulled toward the left pole. Is it under tension?
scenes.visual: Camera pans back up to the hero, still syntelic. Both fibres pull it left (two yellow arrows pointing the same way); the pair drifts left. The empty blue bracket appears between its kinetochores, short and flickering. Question text 'Is it under tension?' appears large.
scenes.narration: Now go back to the syntelic pair. Both sisters are pulled toward the left pole. Is it under tension?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause. Question 'Is it under tension?' stays on screen. The hero keeps drifting slowly left and back; the short blue bracket flickers but does not grow.

scenes.tts: In the rope picture, no. Same-way pulls drag the pair along without stretching it. Real pairs can still bear some load from other forces. So the cell should let go and try again.
scenes.visual: Question fades. The faint rope outline is laid over the hero: both pull arrows on one end, the rope slides without going taut. The blue bracket stays short, label 'little tension' (blue). On 'some load', a small grey push arrow on the arms nudges the pair (no number). On 'let go', the right kinetochore's fibre trembles.
scenes.narration: In the rope picture, no. Same-way pulls drag the pair along without stretching it. Real pairs can still bear some load from other forces. So the cell should let go and try again.

scenes.tts: A kinase called Aurora B sits mostly between the sister kinetochores. It phosphorylates the proteins that grip the fibres, weakening their grip. Slack grips tend to let go and be remade.
scenes.visual: Show then tell: a pink cloud labelled 'Aurora B' (pink) blooms between the hero's two kinetochores. Small pink dots hop out onto the orange kinetochores where the fibres hold. The right kinetochore's wrong fibre loosens and pops off toward the left pole; that kinetochore pulses red. Counter in the panel ticks 'empty kinetochores: 1' to '2', and a second red wave starts toward the purple brake. Meanwhile, unnarrated, two teal rings on the hero's arms drift off (this continues slowly through later scenes until only centromere rings remain).
scenes.narration: A kinase called Aurora B sits mostly between the sister kinetochores. It phosphorylates the proteins that grip the fibres, weakening their grip. Slack grips tend to let go and be remade.

scenes.tts: Under tension, Aurora B weakens the grip less. Force also steadies a grip directly. So taut grips tend to stay.
scenes.visual: A fibre from the RIGHT pole catches the hero's empty kinetochore. The pair swings to the middle; the blue bracket grows long ('tension (schematic)'); the pink dots fade from the kinetochores and the pink cloud dims (the picture makes no claim about how). Counter ticks '2' back to '1' (the stuck one is still empty). The hero's fibres thicken slightly: 'held' (blue).
scenes.narration: Under tension, Aurora B weakens the grip less. Force also steadies a grip directly. So taut grips tend to stay.

scenes.tts: Here is the whole rule. Keep what is pulled from both sides. Remake what is not. And cut only when no kinetochore is left empty.
scenes.visual: Camera pulls out to the full cell. The three phrases appear one at a time, large, each tied to a motion in the world: 'Keep the taut' (blue) as both middle pairs glow along their stretch brackets; 'Remake the slack' (pink) as the stuck one's grip flickers; 'Cut only when none is empty' (red) as the panel lamp pulses WAIT and the counter reads 1. The three lines stack at top left and remain for the scene.
scenes.narration: Here is the whole rule. Keep what is pulled from both sides. Remake what is not. And cut only when no kinetochore is left empty.

scenes.tts: Turning over a wrong grip can leave its kinetochore empty. Empty means without enough end-on attachment. An empty kinetochore sends a wait signal. It holds back the A P C, or anaphase-promoting complex.
scenes.caption: Turning over a wrong grip can leave its kinetochore empty. Empty means without enough end-on attachment. An empty kinetochore sends a wait signal. It holds back the APC, or anaphase-promoting complex.
scenes.visual: The rule text fades. On the hero, the earlier moment flashes once (its right kinetochore red and empty, then caught again). Then the camera settles on THE STUCK ONE near the left pole: a side-on fibre touches its free kinetochore but does not end on it, and the kinetochore keeps pulsing red ('empty', red). The red wave runs to the panel; the purple clamp is relabelled 'APC: anaphase-promoting complex' (purple) and stays clamped.
scenes.narration: Turning over a wrong grip can leave its kinetochore empty. Empty means without enough end-on attachment. An empty kinetochore sends a wait signal. It holds back the APC, or anaphase-promoting complex.

scenes.tts: While even one is empty, the cell waits. In a stuck rat kangaroo cell, Conly Rieder's team destroyed that one empty kinetochore with a laser. About twenty minutes later, anaphase began.
scenes.visual: Panel lamp pulses WAIT. A thin white laser line sweeps in from the top and hits the stuck one's free kinetochore; the orange dot goes dark grey ('destroyed'). The red waves stop. Counter ticks '1' to '0'. A small clock icon in the panel spins, label 'about 20 min later'. The purple clamp releases and the lamp turns green 'GO'. Label at bottom: 'PtK1 cell, 1995' (TEXT).
scenes.narration: While even one is empty, the cell waits. In a stuck rat kangaroo cell, Conly Rieder's team destroyed that one empty kinetochore with a laser. About twenty minutes later, anaphase began.

scenes.tts: The damaged chromosome never reached the middle. So the cell was not waiting for alignment. The wait signal came from in or near that empty kinetochore.
scenes.visual: A dashed white vertical line marks the middle of the spindle. The stuck one stays near the left pole, far from the line (small double-headed grey arrow shows the gap), while the two middle pairs sit on the line. Then a red ring outlines the region around the destroyed kinetochore, label 'signal source: in or near' (red).
scenes.narration: The damaged chromosome never reached the middle. So the cell was not waiting for alignment. The wait signal came from in or near that empty kinetochore.

scenes.tts: A human cell has ninety-two kinetochores before anaphase. Ninety-one are attached. One is empty. Does the cell go?
scenes.caption: A human cell has 92 kinetochores before anaphase. 91 are attached. One is empty. Does the cell go?
scenes.visual: The world refills (relabel 'human cell'): the spindle middle fills with 46 small duplicated chromosomes (schematic), all bioriented and jiggling, the hero still visible among them. Lamp back to red WAIT. Exactly one small kinetochore pulses red. Counter now reads 'attached: 91 of 92'. Question 'Does the cell go?' appears large.
scenes.narration: A human cell has 92 kinetochores before anaphase. 91 are attached. One is empty. Does the cell go?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause. Question stays. The one red kinetochore keeps pulsing; a faint red wave runs to the panel each pulse; the 46 pairs keep jiggling.

scenes.tts: No. One in ninety-two is about one point one percent. A majority vote would miss it. The checkpoint works the other way: any empty kinetochore means wait.
scenes.caption: No. One in 92 is about 1.1 percent. A majority vote would miss it. The checkpoint works the other way: any empty kinetochore means wait.
scenes.visual: Question fades. A thin bar under the counter shows 91 blue slots and 1 red slot to scale, label 'about 1.1%' (red). A crossed-out 'majority vote' (grey strike, red cross) appears and fades. The lamp stays WAIT. Then a fibre finds the last empty kinetochore: counter 'attached: 92 of 92', red waves stop.
scenes.narration: No. One in 92 is about 1.1 percent. A majority vote would miss it. The checkpoint works the other way: any empty kinetochore means wait.

scenes.tts: When none is empty, the brake on the A P C comes off. It tags securin for destruction. Securin had kept an enzyme called separase inactive. Now separase is free.
scenes.caption: When none is empty, the brake on the APC comes off. It tags securin for destruction. Securin had kept an enzyme called separase inactive. Now separase is free.
scenes.visual: Lamp turns green 'GO'; the purple clamp opens and the APC (purple shape) glides from the panel down to the hero's centromere. Parked there since this scene began: a dim green shape 'separase' with a gold shape 'securin' sitting on it, label 'inactive' (red). The APC stamps small purple tag chips onto securin; securin crumbles into gold fragments that fade away. Separase brightens to full green, label changes to 'active' (green).
scenes.narration: When none is empty, the brake on the APC comes off. It tags securin for destruction. Securin had kept an enzyme called separase inactive. Now separase is free.

scenes.tts: Separase is a protease. It cuts one subunit of the cohesin ring, and the ring opens. In vertebrates, the cut acts mainly at the centromere.
scenes.visual: Camera pushes in on the hero's centromere until the teal rings fill the middle of the frame. Separase docks on one teal ring and snips one segment (label 'one subunit', teal); the ring springs open; the next ring is cut the same way. On 'vertebrates', a quick ghost of the hero's earlier arm rings (from s02) flashes along the arms and fades, showing they left earlier (they drifted off during s08 to s16); label 'mainly centromere' (teal).
scenes.narration: Separase is a protease. It cuts one subunit of the cohesin ring, and the ring opens. In vertebrates, the cut acts mainly at the centromere.

scenes.tts: And a cut ring cannot be rejoined. In a normal cycle, sisters are paired only as DNA is copied.
scenes.visual: The two halves of a cut ring drift; a dashed arrow tries to rejoin them and is struck through in red, label 'cannot be rejoined' (red). A one-way arrow (white) appears under the hero, pointing forward only. A small 'next S phase: new sisters' tag (TEXT) slides along the one-way arrow. The sisters begin to pull apart at the centromere.
scenes.narration: And a cut ring cannot be rejoined. In a normal cycle, sisters are paired only as DNA is copied.

scenes.tts: The sisters part. In anaphase A, each moves toward its pole. In anaphase B, the poles themselves move apart.
scenes.visual: Camera pulls out to the full cell. All pairs split; each blue sister travels to its pole. Orange brackets from each of the hero's kinetochores to its pole shrink, label 'anaphase A' (orange). Then a yellow bracket spanning pole to pole grows as the poles slide outward, label 'anaphase B' (yellow). Brackets are schematic; no numbers.
scenes.narration: The sisters part. In anaphase A, each moves toward its pole. In anaphase B, the poles themselves move apart.

scenes.tts: One error slips through. Sometimes one kinetochore is gripped from both poles, called merotelic. It is attached, so it sends no wait signal. The pair is partly under tension, so Aurora B can miss it.
scenes.visual: The world rewinds to metaphase (sisters slide back to the middle, quick reverse motion, small 'rewind' label). One pair in the crowd is highlighted: one of its kinetochores has fibres to BOTH poles, label 'merotelic' (red). Counter reads 'empty kinetochores: 0' and the lamp is green. A faint pink Aurora B cloud between this pair dims under the partial stretch; its blue bracket is medium length ('partial tension', schematic).
scenes.narration: One error slips through. Sometimes one kinetochore is gripped from both poles, called merotelic. It is attached, so it sends no wait signal. The pair is partly under tension, so Aurora B can miss it.

scenes.tts: Anaphase can start on time, error and all. That kinetochore is pulled toward both poles, and its chromatid can lag.
scenes.visual: Anaphase plays again. Every sister goes to its pole except the merotelic one, which is tugged both ways (two yellow arrows on its one kinetochore) and is left behind near the middle line, label 'lagging' (red). New nuclear outlines (grey) start to form around each set at the poles.
scenes.narration: Anaphase can start on time, error and all. That kinetochore is pulled toward both poles, and its chromatid can lag.

scenes.tts: In two human cell lines, most lagging chromosomes rejoined the main nucleus. A minority ended up in a small separate nucleus.
scenes.visual: The lagging chromatid splits into two schematic outcomes side by side (same cell, two ghosted futures): in the larger, it slides late into the main nucleus, label 'most rejoin' (blue); in the smaller, a tiny grey envelope closes around it apart from the main nucleus, label 'micronucleus' (red). No percentages on screen.
scenes.narration: In two human cell lines, most lagging chromosomes rejoined the main nucleus. A minority ended up in a small separate nucleus.

scenes.tts: The checkpoint never reads right or wrong. Tension sorts the grips: taut ones tend to stay, slack ones are remade. It just waits until no kinetochore is empty. Then one cut, and the sisters part for good.
scenes.visual: Fast recap as motion in the same world, each beat on its sentence: the hero's blue bracket stretches taut and holds; a slack grip pops off and is re-caught (pink flash); the panel lamp flips WAIT to GO as the counter reaches 0; separase snips the last teal ring and two daughter nuclei close (grey outlines) at the poles. Slow drift continues.
scenes.narration: The checkpoint never reads right or wrong. Tension sorts the grips: taut ones tend to stay, slack ones are remade. It just waits until no kinetochore is empty. Then one cut, and the sisters part for good.

scenes.visual: End card
scenes.line: Keep taut grips, remake slack ones, cut when none is empty.
